summary: This document revises, extends, and replaces RFC 6622. It describes flexible TLVs for cryptographic Integrity Check Values and timestamps, using the MANET packet and message format from RFC 5444. It defines Packet, Message, and Address Block TLVs.

plainLanguage.summary: Messages in a wireless group need a tamper seal and a time stamp. This defines a standard way to attach both.

questions: what is an icv tlv in manet
what is the timestamp tlv in rfc 5444
what does icv type extension 2 cover
how is an icv calculated for a manet message
subtitle: Standard TLVs for attaching integrity check values and timestamps to MANET packets, messages and addresses.

tldr.problem: MANET routing protocols that use the RFC 5444 packet format need a common way to carry cryptographic integrity checks and freshness information, because security needs vary widely between deployments.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines an ICV TLV and a TIMESTAMP TLV, each as a Packet, Message and Address Block TLV, plus type extensions, a hash function plus cryptographic function layout for the ICV value, and rules for what the ICV covers.
tldr.outcome: It is a framework, not a protocol: routing protocols and their extensions choose how to use it. It obsoletes RFC 6622 and adds ICV type extension 2, which also covers the IP source address.

today: RFC 7182 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 6622, and no later RFC obsoletes or updates it. It remains a framework that MANET routing protocols and their extensions reference.

sections.title: Introduction and Scope
sections.content:
RFC 7182 gives a syntax for security-related information in RFC 5444 addresses, messages and packets, and registers TLV types and type extension registries for them. It is not a stand-alone protocol. It is intended for use by MANET routing protocols or their security extensions, which must say how to handle packets, messages and addresses that carry such information.

The document revises, extends and replaces RFC 6622. Key management and key exchange are out of scope. Two kinds of TLV are specified: one for Integrity Check Values (ICVs) and one for timestamps, each usable in packets, messages and Address Blocks.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a set of building blocks for adding a tamper seal and a time stamp to messages. It is not a whole system by itself.

sections.title: The Security Architecture
sections.content:
The RFC starts from the observation that in MANET security "one size rarely fits all"; deployment domains range from "unbreakable" to "virtually none". So routing protocols such as NHDP (RFC 6130) and OLSRv2 (RFC 7181) stay generic and allow a message to be rejected as "badly formed" or "insecure", for example when an ICV fails to verify.

Security extensions then do the rejecting that suits their domain. This document supplies the third piece: code points and a common exchange format for ICVs and timestamps, reserved from the TLV registries of RFC 5444.
sections.plainLanguage: Different networks need different amounts of safety. So the basic rules stay simple, and each network adds the level of locking it needs, using shared seals and stamps.

sections.title: The ICV and TIMESTAMP TLVs
sections.content:
The ICV TLV value is one or more <ICV-value> fields, and the TIMESTAMP TLV value is one or more <time-value> fields. In a multivalue Address Block TLV each value has the single-length instead of the whole <length>. How a value is computed and structured is set by the TLV's type extension.

A timestamp is essentially freshness information. Its meaning is decided by the routing protocol that uses it and may be a POSIX timestamp, a GPS timestamp or a simple sequence number. The RFC notes that time synchronisation in a MANET may be difficult and does not specify a mechanism for it.

Type extension 0 for ICV is a basic ICV: a plain sequence of octets with no specified structure. How it is calculated and which parameters are needed is established outside this specification, for example by administrative configuration.
sections.plainLanguage: An ICV is the seal on the envelope, and a timestamp says when it was sealed. The TLV is just the label that holds each one.

sections.title: Packets, Messages and Address Blocks
sections.content:
Each of the two TLVs exists in three forms, with these rules for calculating the ICV.

  • Packet TLVs: existing ICV Packet TLVs are removed before the calculation and restored afterwards, and the Packet TLV Block size is recalculated. If no Packet TLVs remain, the empty block is removed and the phastlv bit is cleared. Packets are never forwarded, so mutable fields need no special care.
  • Message TLVs: <msg-hop-limit> and <msg-hop-count>, if present, are assumed to be 0 during the calculation, because routers change them as they forward. Existing ICV Message TLVs are removed and restored in the same way.
  • Address Block TLVs: the ICV covers one or more addresses concatenated with other associated values. It must not include ICV Address Block TLVs already associated with those addresses. The routing protocol must specify how to include other attributes.

Removing earlier ICVs makes it possible to add several ICVs, for example with different functions, to the same object. TIMESTAMP TLVs, and any other TLVs, must be added before the ICV TLVs so the ICV covers them.
sections.plainLanguage: Before sealing, you take off any older seals so they do not get mixed in. Things that change on the way, like a hop counter, count as zero so the seal still matches at the other end.

sections.title: ICV with a Hash and a Cryptographic Function
sections.content:
Type extensions 1 and 2 give the ICV value a defined structure: <hash-function>, <cryptographic-function> and <key-id-length>, each one octet, then an optional <key-id> and the <ICV-data>. A key identifier length of zero is reserved for a single pre-installed shared key, in which case no key identifier is present. Unless otherwise specified, the ICV is the cryptographic function applied to the hash of the content; HMAC is a noted exception that uses the hash function twice.

The difference between the two extensions is that extension 2 also covers the source address of the IP datagram, represented as one octet of address length followed by the address in network byte order. This protects links in protocols such as NHDP that use that address without always carrying it in the payload. It applies only to one-hop packets and messages, not to forwarded messages such as TC messages in OLSRv2.

The <ICV-data> may be truncated, but HMAC output must not be truncated below 4 octets and the NIST guidance must be followed. The length must also make a dictionary attack improbable. The RFC gives a worked example in which 32 routers, 1000 verifications per second, one day and a probability of 10^-6 require at least 52 bits. Parameters, such as RSASSA-PSS with exponent 65537 for RSA, AES-CMAC for AES, and a hash pinned to the curve for ECDSA, are chosen administratively and exchanged with the keys.
sections.plainLanguage: The seal records which scrambling recipe and which key were used, so the receiver knows how to check it. A shorter seal is easier to forge, so it must not be too short.

sections.title: IANA Registries
sections.content:
The TLV types are the same in all three contexts: type 5 is ICV and type 6 is TIMESTAMP, allocated from the Packet, Message and Address Block TLV Type registries of RFC 5444. Each type has its own type extension registry, replacing those from RFC 6622. Extensions 3 to 251 are Unassigned with Expert Review, and 252 to 255 are reserved for experimental use.

Timestamp type extensions are 0 (unsigned, arbitrary length), 1 (unsigned 32-bit POSIX), 2 (NTP format) and 3 (signed, arbitrary length with no constraints such as monotonicity). More than one ICV TLV with the same extension may be included if they represent different calculations, but more than one TIMESTAMP TLV with the same extension must not be.

Two further registries cover the hash functions (0 none, 1 SHA-1, 2 SHA-224, 3 SHA-256, 4 SHA-384, 5 SHA-512) and the cryptographic functions (0 none, 1 RSA, 2 DSA, 3 HMAC, 4 3DES, 5 AES, 6 ECDSA).
sections.plainLanguage: There is an official list of numbers for each kind of seal, stamp and scrambling recipe. That way everyone uses the same number for the same thing.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Because the document is not a protocol, it has the same security considerations as RFC 5444. A routing protocol or extension that uses it must specify how it uses the framework and describe the protection it gets.

For example, a protocol that rejects messages without a valid ICV should state the assumption that a valid ICV means a valid message. It should also list the problems this counters, such as link or identity spoofing, and those it does not, such as compromised keys.
sections.plainLanguage: Whoever uses these seals must say what they protect against and what they do not, so nobody trusts them too much.

sections.title: Differences from RFC 6622
sections.content:
Compared with RFC 6622, this document adds ICV type extension 2, which keeps the structure of extension 1 but also covers the IP datagram source address. It clarifies that an ICV may be truncated and that one multivalue ICV or TIMESTAMP Address Block TLV can cover more than one address. It also renames the TLVs, for example from "Packet ICV TLV" to "ICV Packet TLV", to match RFC 5444.

One normative change turns a SHOULD into a MUST: TIMESTAMP TLVs, and any other Message TLVs, must be added to a message before its ICV TLVs.
sections.plainLanguage: This is the updated edition. It adds one more kind of seal and makes one tip into a firm rule.

fields.desc: Hash function from the IANA registry.

fields.name: Cryptographic Function
fields.desc: Cryptographic function from the IANA registry.

fields.name: Key ID Length
fields.desc: Length of the key ID in octets; 0 means a single pre-installed shared key.

fields.name: Key ID (optional)
fields.desc: Present only if the length is not zero; then the ICV data follows.
